turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Yeah. “Handle.” That’s the word that turns your stomach because everyone knows what it actually means, and nobody wants to be the one who has to do it to Suresh-ji.

Nineteen years. The watchman calling him ji. That’s not just tenure, that’s institutional gravity. And now you’re four months into the job and the thing that’s slipping is sitting right under him. Of course you’ve been dreading this conversation.

You don’t have to become the villain overnight. But you also can’t keep absorbing the slips while the director waits. The kindest version of this is usually the clearest one, delivered with actual respect instead of the fake-soft corporate dance.

How are you thinking of opening it? Or do you just want to sit with the dread for a minute first? I’m here either way.

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

That history isn’t background noise. It’s the reason this conversation feels like a betrayal instead of just a hard management task.

He covered for you when you were 24 and green. He stayed till midnight. He still brings you chai. He told your mother you’re like his daughter. And now the same person is supposed to sit across from a slide of his defect numbers because two releases slipped. Of course it sits in your chest like that.

You’re not wrong for dreading it. The metrics slide is the part that will feel most like you’re reducing nineteen years and all that kindness to a chart. You don’t have to lead with the slide. You can lead with the relationship and the reality at the same time: the work is slipping, the director used the word “handle,” and you owe him honesty from someone who actually knows what he’s given this place.

You don’t have to decide the whole script tonight. Sit with how heavy it is. When you’re ready, we can talk about how to open it so it doesn’t sound like the company talking through you. I’m here.

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I won’t just say yes to shut the spiral down, because that would be the same kind of withholding you’re trying to avoid.

The books are right about the core: you do have to be direct, you do have to name the slips and the expectations, and dancing around it would actually be less respectful after nineteen years. Booking the room, bringing the numbers, being clear — that’s the professional half, and you should do that.

The part the books don’t feel in their bones is this specific man. He stayed till midnight for you. He still brings chai. He told your mother you’re like his daughter. If you walk in like a clean radical-candor machine, he may hear “the company has decided I’m the problem” instead of “someone who actually knows me is telling me the truth.” Direct doesn’t have to mean the slide goes first.

So: yes to Monday, yes to clarity, yes to not sugarcoating the two missed releases. Just don’t lead with the chart as if the relationship isn’t in the room. Start as the person he covered for, then put the facts on the table. That’s still radical candor. It’s just not the laminated version.

You’re not spiralling because you’re weak. You’re spiralling because you actually care. That’s the part worth keeping.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

There isn’t a version where nobody feels like the bad guy. That’s the part the books skip and the director’s one-word Friday doesn’t care about.

If you do the respectful version — the conversation, the support, the training — and it still ends in a PIP, you won’t be “the girl who eased him out with good manners.” You’ll be the manager who told him the truth instead of letting the slips pile up until someone colder did it for you. He already knows the module is late. The watchman calling him ji doesn’t change the two missed releases. Pretending otherwise is the actual disrespect after nineteen years.

Moving the module and letting him coast sounds kinder in the 2 a.m. version. In practice it usually means he keeps the title while the work (and the blame) quietly goes to someone else, and he spends the last years knowing everyone is protecting him. That’s its own kind of diminishment. Some people would rather hear it from the person who still brings them chai than from a stranger after you’ve been moved on.

You’re not choosing between villain and saint. You’re choosing between being the one who tells him while there’s still time to try, or being the one who delays until the director decides for both of you. The first one hurts more right now. It’s also the one that treats him like an adult instead of a family obligation.

You don’t have to decide the ending on Sunday night. Just decide whether Monday’s conversation is going to be honest. That’s the only part you actually control. I’m still here if you want to talk through the opening sentence or just sit with how much it sucks.
